name: AI Customer Support Agent
oneLiner: Decides which messages an agent should answer, what it must be told, what it must never say — and how often it has to be right before it saves any money.
audience: Anyone about to put an AI agent on their support inbox
Agencies selling support automation to clients
Support leads asked to justify a bot to a finance team
problem: Support agents are sold on containment: the share of conversations the bot closes. Containment counts the tickets it answers and ignores the ones it answers wrongly, which do not cost zero — the customer comes back crosser, a person untangles it, and some of them leave. Once you count that, the whole case changes, and it changes per intent rather than for 'support' as a whole.
solves: Automating 'support' as one undifferentiated thing
Business cases built on containment with no cost attached to wrong answers
Agents with no explicit refusal list, improvising on refunds and legal questions
Going live with no test bench, so the first regression is found by a customer
inside: Intent-by-intent analysis — which of your messages are safe to automate and which are not
The accuracy threshold: how often it must be right before it saves money at your volumes
A system prompt generated from your policies, not a template
Fixed replies for the intents that must never be improvised
A 50-case test bench, including the ones designed to make it fail
A rollout plan with gates that refuse to open until the tests pass
outcomes: A list of intents to automate and a list to leave alone, each with a reason
The accuracy figure the project must hit to be worth doing
A system prompt and a refusal list you can hand to whoever builds it
usage: Open index.html and enter your ticket volume, mix and the cost of a human reply.
Work through the intents. The ones it advises against automating are the point.
Read the accuracy threshold before committing to a build.
Generate the system prompt and the fixed replies; edit the policies to match yours exactly.
Run the 50-case bench against the built agent before any rollout gate opens.
notFor: Anyone wanting a working chatbot — nothing here talks to a model
Teams that have already built and only need hosting
proof: It is a planning tool. The economics are computed from your volumes and costs; the accuracy has to be measured against the bench once something exists.

name: AI Appointment Booking System
tagline: A booking agent that invents a Tuesday looks fine
oneLiner: A timezone-correct availability engine, the agent's prompt and tools generated from your own services and policies, and a simulator that books against the real engine.
audience: Clinics, salons, garages and studios automating their diary
Coaches with clients in other time zones
Agencies selling booking automation to local businesses
problem: 'An AI books your appointments' is the easiest local automation to sell and the easiest to get badly wrong, because it fails quietly. A booking agent that invents a Tuesday looks exactly like one that checked. Nobody finds out until somebody drives to an appointment that was never in the diary — and by then the client has lost trust in the whole idea.
solves: Agents that hallucinate availability because nothing constrains them
Timezone arithmetic done in the prompt, which is where it goes wrong
Prompts, tool definitions and customer messages drifting out of agreement
Message templates that exceed an SMS segment and cost triple
inside: A timezone-correct availability engine: opening hours, breaks, buffers, lead times, holidays
The system prompt and tool definitions generated from the same configuration, so they cannot disagree
A conversation simulator that books against the real engine, not a mock
Message templates counted in SMS segments
Policies — cancellation, no-show, deposits — expressed once and reflected everywhere
The wiring guide for connecting it to a real calendar
outcomes: An availability engine you can test before anything is built
A prompt and tool schema that match the engine exactly
Messages that fit one SMS segment and say what the policy actually is
usage: Open index.html and configure services, hours, buffers and time zone.
Use the simulator to book across a timezone boundary and a holiday — that is where these break.
Generate the prompt and tool definitions together; never edit one alone.
Check every message template's segment count before you approve it.
Follow the wiring guide to connect a real calendar.
notFor: Anyone wanting a running booking bot — this is the specification for one
Complex resource scheduling across many rooms and staff constraints
proof: The engine is real and testable in the simulator. Whether the model you eventually connect obeys the tools is a property of that model, not of this file.

name: WhatsApp AI Sales Assistant
tagline: The 24-hour window decides what you may send
oneLiner: Turns 'we should put AI on our WhatsApp' into a build spec: qualification playbook, prompt, templates checked against platform rules, and the cost model.
audience: Businesses selling in a chat window rather than on a website
Agencies building WhatsApp automations for clients
Anyone whose template messages keep getting rejected
problem: On WhatsApp the selling is the easy half. The half that sinks these builds is a set of platform rules: what a template may say, when a session is open, what a follow-up is allowed to be once the 24-hour window closes, and what each conversation category costs. Get those wrong and your templates are rejected, your follow-ups never arrive, and the per-conversation bill arrives anyway.
solves: Template messages rejected for reasons nobody explains
Follow-ups sent outside the 24-hour window that silently do nothing
Conversation costs discovered on the first invoice
Assistants that qualify nobody and hand every chat to a human anyway
inside: A qualification playbook — what to ask, in what order, and when to hand over
A system prompt and a knowledge file generated from your own offer and policies
Message templates checked against the platform's content rules before you submit them
The 24-hour window arithmetic that decides what each follow-up may legally be
A cost model per conversation category, at your volume
The conversion lift the whole build must earn to be worth doing
outcomes: Templates that pass review the first time
A follow-up schedule that respects the window instead of hoping
A number for the conversion lift required before you commit
usage: Open index.html and describe your offer and qualification criteria.
Draft templates in the checker; fix what it flags before submitting to Meta.
Model your conversation volume and read the monthly cost.
Compare that against the required conversion lift. If the lift is implausible, stop here.
Hand the prompt, knowledge file and templates to whoever builds it.
notFor: Anyone wanting the bot itself — this is the specification
Bulk messaging or anything resembling unsolicited broadcast
proof: Platform rules and pricing change without notice. The checker encodes them as of writing; re-read Meta's current policy before you submit templates.

name: AI Real Estate Agent
tagline: Leads are not lost to competitors, but to Tuesday
oneLiner: Which enquiries the assistant answers first, what it asks, what it must never say, and whether the arithmetic works at your lead volume — with a fair-housing checker.
audience: Estate agents buying portal leads and losing them to response time
Property businesses automating first response
Agencies building assistants for property clients
problem: Agents buy leads and then lose them to the clock — not to a competitor with a better CRM, but to a Tuesday evening, a valuation that overran, and a portal enquiry that sat unanswered until Thursday. And the unit of decision is the source, not 'leads': a portal enquiry and a past-client referral share a name and nothing else.
solves: Portal enquiries answered two days late, when the lead has already booked elsewhere
Treating every lead source identically when their values differ by an order of magnitude
Automated copy that strays into fair-housing violations
Rollouts with no test bench and no gate, going live on hope
inside: Source-by-source analysis, because a portal lead and a referral are different products
What a lost lead actually costs, computed at your volume and conversion
A system prompt and qualification scripts generated from your own stock and policies
A hard refusal list — valuations, legal advice, anything it must not say
A 46-case test bench covering the awkward cases
A fair-housing copy checker
A rollout plan with gates that refuse to open
outcomes: A response-time target with money attached to it
A prompt and script set specific to each lead source
Copy checked against fair-housing language before it reaches a member of the public
usage: Open index.html and enter lead volumes and conversion by source.
Read the cost of a lost lead per source. It reorders priorities immediately.
Generate prompts and scripts for the highest-value source first.
Run every piece of customer-facing copy through the fair-housing checker.
Do not open a rollout gate until the 46-case bench passes.
notFor: Anyone wanting a working assistant — nothing here talks to a model
Legal compliance sign-off; the checker is an aid, not an approval
proof: The fair-housing checker flags language patterns. It is not legal advice and does not certify compliance — have a qualified person review anything public.

name: AI Website + CRM Automation
tagline: At thirty enquiries a month, most of the build list is a hobby
oneLiner: The site page by page, the CRM pipeline stage by stage, the tool stack with its running cost — and, per automation, whether your volume pays for building it.
audience: Agencies selling website-and-CRM builds to local businesses
Business owners quoted for a forty-automation build
Anyone whose CRM has twelve custom fields and no one filling them
problem: Website and CRM automation is the most saleable service there is, and it is where the largest amount of confident nonsense lives: build lists of forty automations, tool stacks priced like an enterprise, and payback claims nobody has ever checked. At thirty enquiries a month most of that build list is a hobby — which is knowable in advance, from arithmetic.
solves: Forty-automation build lists sold to businesses with thirty enquiries a month
Tool stacks whose monthly cost nobody totalled
Pipeline stages copied from a template and never matched to how deals actually move
Automations built in the order they were thought of
inside: The site planned page by page for your business model
A CRM pipeline stage by stage, with the fields each stage genuinely needs
Automation recipes per business model, each with a payback calculation at your volume
A tool stack with its real monthly running cost totalled
Message templates for each automated touchpoint
A verdict per automation: build now, build later, or do not build
outcomes: A build list ordered by payback rather than by enthusiasm
A monthly tool cost you knew before signing up to anything
A pipeline that matches how your deals actually move
usage: Open index.html and pick your business model, then enter monthly enquiry volume and your hourly rate.
Read the 'do not build yet' list carefully — it is usually most of the list.
Total the tool stack cost before subscribing to anything.
Build the top three automations only, then re-run the arithmetic.
Use the templates as the starting text for each touchpoint.
notFor: Anyone wanting the automations built — this decides which ones deserve building
proof: Payback is computed from your volume and your hourly rate. Change either and the build list changes — which is the point.

name: E-Commerce Order Automation
tagline: 159 hours a month nobody invoices you for
oneLiner: Costs an order desk minute by minute, ranks every automation by how fast it repays, turns exception handling into arithmetic, and exports the runbook.
audience: Store owners whose order desk quietly consumes the week
Anyone about to hire for fulfilment admin
Agencies automating operations for e-commerce clients
problem: A store's order desk is the part that scales worst. A listing is written once; an order is processed every single time, and the minutes are invisible — nobody invoices you for reading the order, checking the payment, picking, packing, buying postage, answering 'where is it?', or reconciling the payout. At ordinary figures a store doing 600 orders a month spends about 159 hours on it.
solves: Fulfilment admin that never appears in any cost calculation
Automations chosen by what is easiest to build rather than what repays first
Exceptions handled by mood, so the same problem costs a different amount each time
No runbook, so the desk stops when the person who runs it is away
inside: A minute-by-minute cost model of the order desk at your volume
Every automation ranked by payback period
Exception handling as decision rules: refunds, damages, missing parcels, chargebacks
The threshold volumes at which each automation starts to make sense
A hiring-versus-automating comparison on the same figures
An exportable runbook you can hand to whoever covers the desk
outcomes: The true monthly hour cost of your order desk
An automation order with payback attached to each item
A runbook that lets someone else run the desk on the day you cannot
usage: Open index.html and enter your monthly order volume and the steps you really perform.
Read the total hours. It is usually the moment the case makes itself.
Take the top-ranked automation only, build it, then re-measure.
Turn the exception rules into policy and stop re-deciding them.
Export the runbook and store it where a stand-in can find it.
proof: The default figures are a starting point; replace them with your own timings. The whole model is only as honest as the minutes you enter.

name: AI Commercial Production Kits
tagline: Whether generating it is worth what it costs
oneLiner: One brief becomes a production kit — script with beat timings, shot list with risk flags, generation prompts, deliverable specs and a clearance checklist.
audience: Anyone quoted for an AI-generated video commercial
Small agencies adding video without a crew
Founders deciding between AI generation, stock, and a shoot
problem: AI video is sold on capability and bought on cost, and the two are rarely compared in the same document. Generation credits, re-rolls for the shots that never come out right, licensing, voice, and the editing that stitches it together add up to a number nobody computes until afterwards — by which point the alternative, which was often stock or a phone camera, is no longer on the table.
solves: Committing to AI video without costing the re-rolls
Shot lists with no risk flags, so the impossible shots are discovered mid-production
Generation prompts written ad hoc, producing inconsistent looks across a single spot
No clearance checklist — music, likeness, trademarks discovered at delivery
inside: A script with beat timings that fit the actual slot length
A shot list with risk flags on the shots AI generation reliably fails
Generation prompts per shot, written to hold a consistent look
Deliverable specs per placement — aspect ratios, durations, safe areas
A clearance checklist covering music, likeness and trademarks
Cost arithmetic comparing generation, stock and a small shoot
outcomes: A verdict on whether generating this particular spot is worth it
A shot list where the hard shots are flagged before anyone starts
Deliverables that fit each placement without a re-export
usage: Open index.html and write the brief: product, audience, slot length, placements.
Read the cost comparison before generating anything.
Work the shot list and pay attention to the risk flags — those are the re-roll budget.
Use the per-shot prompts to keep the look consistent.
Run the clearance checklist before delivery, not after.
notFor: Anyone expecting video to be generated here — this is the production kit
proof: Generation pricing moves constantly. Update the per-second costs before you rely on the comparison.
